summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed dismissal of a former foster child's section 1983 claims, holding that a child removed from his home on allegedly fabricated neglect allegations stated Fourth Amendment and substantive due process claims that survived the defendants' immunity defenses in part.
key_cases.relevance: The foundational Seventh Circuit decision on unlawful removal of an Illinois child under section 1983.
key_cases.quote: a seizure is reasonable if it is pursuant to a court order, if it is supported by probable cause, or if it is justified by exigent circumstances

key_cases.case_name: Hernandez ex rel. Hernandez v. Foster
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity on the initial removal of an Illinois child but vacated as to continuing to hold him after probable cause dissipated and as to the coerced safety plan, remanding those claims for further proceedings.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Illinois-specific authority on section 1983 liability for removal and continued withholding of a child.
key_cases.quote: Probable cause is determined on the basis of the facts and circumstances known to the defendants at the time of the conduct in issue

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of qualified immunity, holding that a caseworker's under-the-clothes examination of children at a private school exceeded the principal's consent to interview them and violated their clearly established Fourth Amendment rights.
key_cases.relevance: Bodily searches of children during an investigation, without consent or a warrant, expose caseworkers to section 1983 liability.
key_cases.quote: the searches of the children's bodies to investigate child abuse were presumptively unreasonable, unless they fall within an exception to the warrant requirement of the Fourth Amendment

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that Illinois violated due process and equal protection by declaring the children of an unwed father dependent without any hearing on his fitness, and reversed the Illinois Supreme Court.
key_cases.relevance: Removal without any hearing on parental fitness is itself the constitutional violation the Court identified in Illinois practice.
key_cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers who searched a private religious school and seized a student for a child-abuse interview without a warrant, court order, probable cause, consent or exigent circumstances violated the Fourth Amendment and the family's right to familial relations, but affirmed qualified immunity because those rights were not yet clearly established.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that seizing a child at school and threatening removal without articulable evidence of abuse are constitutional violations, the analysis Michael C. v. Gresbach later applies.
key_cases.quote: although child welfare caseworkers may investigate allegations of child abuse without violating parents' constitutional right to familial relations, they may not do so arbitrarily

key_cases.case_name: Siliven v. Indiana Department of Child Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for the caseworkers, holding that a removal made without a court order is reasonable only if supported by probable cause or exigent circumstances and that a physician's opinion of inflicted injury plus a prior abuse allegation supplied probable cause here.
key_cases.relevance: The source of the probable-cause timing rule that Hernandez draws on and that governs section 1983 removal claims in this circuit.
key_cases.quote: The pertinent inquiry, then, is whether defendants had probable cause to believe that C.S.'s physical health would be seriously endangered if he was not immediately removed from his father's custody.
